abstract: Throughout history, men have been making models of the physical events they observe. From cave pictures to surrealist art, from models of the atom to models of the universe, all have sought to focus attention on particular ideas for analysis or for communication to other people. As engineers, we must be particularly skilled in the art of making or choosing the mathematical models of our engineering concepts. Desirable properties of a model, such as the enchancement of areas for which analysis is required and rejection of areas of no interest, seem obvious. However, the computational power at the fingertips of the professional engineer is increasing enormously through the proliferation of calculators and computers. Thus the methods for analysing models are changing, and this means that the models we have chosen in the past may not always be the best for the present and future

articleTitle: Amorphous ribbon materials and their possibilities
abstract: The magnetic properties of a new type of material, the amorphous alloys, appear to have advantages over those of existing magnetic materials, e.g. lower power loss. But the new material is not yet completely acceptable. The present research and development programme is aimed principally at improving dimensional quality, increasing saturation flux density and lowering the power loss further, all of which should make the new material commercially viable in the 1980s

articleTitle: Silicone liquid filled transformersߝthe next five years
abstract: Over the last five years, extensive operating experience has been built up with distribution transformers using silicone liquids. But the transformers were made to conventional designs for other liquids. As the properties of silicone liquids are different, there is considerable scope for new designs

articleTitle: Industry and education a love ߝ hate relationship
abstract: The close relation between industry and higher education results both in cooperation and misunderstanding. The majority of new entrants to the electrical engineering profession receive no formal training, and this can only be corrected by industry. Most British professional engineers are also undereducated, but this can be remedied by the universities if industry will support postgraduate education

articleTitle: Memory testing. characterisation timing and patterns
abstract: Semiconductor memory testing is of growing importance to manufacturers of electronic equipment. Memories are being designed into a surprising number of different types of electronic equipment, and so the memory content of end products continues to expand. Also memory complexity, and the complexity of the printed-circuit boards to which they are attached, is increasing. All these factors emphasise the need for memory testing

articleTitle: F.C. Williams. his contribution to the development of automatic control
Engineering planning of the BBC's electronic news gathering system
abstract: In October 1978 the BBC completed a one year experiment designed to assess the production, engineering and logistic problems in mounting an electronic-news-gathering operation in London. This article deals with some aspects of the engineering planning and system design to which we devoted most attention, and concentrates particularly on the radio link

The possibility of using controlled direct-current electromagnets to support large weights was demonstrated by Kemper in 1932. However, it was only in the mid-1960s, with the advent of high-power solid-state devices, the full potential of electromagnetic suspension was realised. The progress that followed was so rapid that, within the next six years, the idea of using magnetic suspension for transportation progressed from `way out' to `a strong contender'. The evolution of several kinds of magnetic suspension is still proceeding with no indication that the ideal compromise to satisfy the many conflicting requirements has been reached. Because of the exciting possibilities, there is a high level of activity in magnetic suspension in Canada, Japan and W. Germany, with lesser efforts in other countries, including the United Kingdom. Some of the basic control problems associated with the electromagnetic suspension system are discussed in this article, and the case for its use in urban and intercity transport systems presented

The assignment of colour images to data obtained during remote-sensing investigations has enabled the human observer to make easier and alternative diagnostic interpretations that may not be apparent in grey-scale representation. `False colour' has been used to display infrared and other nonoptical imagery to advantage, and similar ideas can be applied to the representation of microwave fields

By systematically introducing the principles of energy conservation and recovery, and the use of solar and wind power, energy-independent houses can be built, even in cloudy Britain. In fact, a Cambridge team have designed a house that would be completely independent of all mains services

Marketing is far too important just to leave to the marketing people, because the way a company markets its products or services directly affects its prospects of profitable survival. Therefore an understanding of the basic components of marketing is important to all of us. Our jobs depend on it

The use of submarine power cables to transmit electrical energy is by no means new, but it will become more common in the future. They will have to be used to transmit power to and from offshore `Islands' that might be developed to extract minerals or energy from the vast potential of the sea. And the technology and experience gained during today's projects, like the cross-Channel 2GW link, will provide a sound basis on which to bulld

To judge from the amount of attention that has been focused on robotics in the technical Press recently, it seems reasonable to predict a large increase in their use in British industry over the next ten years. Robots are being introduced to the world's manufacturing industry because of their low economic wage (sometimes less than £1 per hour), they work 98% of their lives and they can be both faster and more accurate under conditions that humans would find intolerable

articleTitle: Perinatal deathߞtwo microprocessor applications that may help to reduce its incidence
abstract: The perinatal death rate is still too high. For every 1000 deliveries in England in 1975, there were 19 deaths during the period between the start of labour and the seventh day of life. Eight of these deaths occurred after birth. All work towards lowering the risk is of benefit, and may contribute to the gradual decline in perinatal mortality that has been seen since records began

Solar energy is freely and readily available but its collection and conversion is capital intensive. Although the technical feasibility of harnessing solar energy has been demonstrated in many areas, efficient economic exploitation has yet to be achieved. But with the current scale of research and development, we may optimistically expect that several of the solar technologies now being investigated will prove successful in providing power on both the small and large scale

articleTitle: Fundamental arc properties for the design of gas-blast circuit-breaker test heads
abstract: Although the design of gas-blast-circuit-breaker test heads involves a compromise between a number of constraints that are imposed by widely different considerations, the inherent performance capability of such test heads should, in principle, be predictable from a knowledge of the dominant arc-plasma processes. Sufficient, although still incomplete, knowledge of these arc processes now exists for the feasibility to be examined of establishing a test-head design process, based on fundamental plasma properties

His headmaster said he would never make a success out of anything, he was expelled from school at the age of 15, and the only way he could get a job was by a friend pulling some strings behind the scenes. Such was the inconspicuous start Albert Einstein made to a brilliant career in science. The advances he was to make over the next 60 years can be matched only by those of Newton two centuries before, and his theories of relativity shook the very foundations of 20th century science. He challenged the absoluteness of space and time in his papers of 1905 (when he was only 26), and his General Theory of 1915 still forms the basis of our current understanding of gravitation

Information is wispy elusive stuff, although that has never prevented engineers from setting about handling it; indeed, it gave rise to one of the first applications of electricity, and the IEE began as `The Society of Telegraph Engineers'. Today, after years of tranquil obsolescence, telegraph engineering has returned to fashion as everyone, reading the writing on the wall, tries to get into the pulsating all-digital act

articleTitle: Getting the sackߝdismissal and the law
abstract: That sinking feeling that you are about to be fired, or that embarrassing moment when you sack the incompetent fellow on the production line ߝ are these part of your experience? If they are, or might be in the future, you might like to have at hand a map plotting the tricky terrain of the law of dismissal

Most modern highly serviced buildings use electronics in a number of applications, often in the control and monitoring of mechanical services plant, internal communication and, more recently, in the automatic balancing of artificial light with daylight. In addition to special applications of these functions, the National Theatre uses electronics in specially developed stage lighting, sound and stage engineering installations to provide the theatre technician and scene designer with the benefits of simple operations, memory, information display and servocontrol

articleTitle: A management information system for power system studies
abstract: The South African Electricity Supply Commission has developed a data-management system for power-system studies. By using a single command language, an engineer can obtain, via the data-base management system, the data describing a particular power system network. The data-base facilities enable the engineer to store and maintain his power-system data, either interactively or via a batch-processing system. This package has been used for a number of years, and has proved to be a valuable tool for both planning and the operation of power-system networks

articleTitle: Mechanical aspects in the design of distribution switchgear
abstract: In an electrical distribution system, switchgear is necessary to control the flow of power either at the command of the operating personnel, or automatically under the discrimination of the protective system to disconnect an unhealthy section on the occurrence of a fault. Its function is thus purely electrical but its design, manufacture and reliability in service depends to a large extent on the correct application of mechanical engineering principles and practice

articleTitle: A transistor pulse-width modulated permanent-magnet motor
abstract: Progress can be said to be the art of extracting further advantage from existing technology. To be really effective, progress comes from the recognition of the inherent characteristics in a design and their application to the problem in a manner that enhances the positive and minimises the negative. This concept can be seen in the development of variable-speed drives, and in particular in the area of small-power electrical machines

Psychical research is a strange subject (and the study and investigation of extra-sensory perception (e.s.p.) is part of it) in that it sometimes leads to a phenomenon to which few other subjects do - the holding of firm opinions in an almost complete absence of knowledge about it. Views about it sometimes seem to be based on a feeling that we know all the laws of nature and that claimed facts that do not fit must be wrong: that e.s.p. cannot occur and therefore that it does not occur. It is hardly necessary to point out to professional engineers how totally unreasonable and unscientific such prejudgments are. Each question must be settled by appealing to the facts rather than to a priori reasoning. This principle is at the heart and core of modern science

Over the last ten years, materials scientists have improved greatly the control of properties of semiconductors and have increased the range of materials available. This has been achieved by refining basic methods and using new techniques of growing semiconductor crystals

articleTitle: Simplifying the calibration of digital voltmeters
abstract: Calibration is, undoubtedly, one of the biggest headaches for the user of accurate digital voltmeters. As the measurement capability of digital voltmeters has increased over the last decade, a corresponding increase in the complexity of the calibration sequence has resulted. New technology has now permitted manual calibration to be replaced by a simple, unskilled, procedure taking a fraction of the time previously required. The calibration system described also has a remote, fully automatic, capability

articleTitle: The early days of British computers - 2
abstract: This article continues the story from the immediate post-war developments at NPL and the Cambridge and Manchester computers already discussed in Part 1, which was published in Electronics & Power, 1978, 24, pp. 827 - 832. It will be remembered that Alan Turing's 1946 design for an Automatic Computing Engine ran into difficulties, not least because the design itself and Turing's personality were incompatible with the other early British computer groups

articleTitle: Control and monitoring of broadcasting transmitters
abstract: To operate a broadcast transmitter network automatically requires the use of instrumentation for the control and monitoring of outstation equipment as well as for the acquisition and reporting of fault information. The BBC has two monitoring centres designed to do these tasks: the first came into service in 1975, the second in April 1978. Only four stations are needed to cover Britain and Northern Ireland

articleTitle: Designing reliable computer systems-the fault-tolerant approach - 2
abstract: This article is the second part of a two-part tutorial article on the design of fault-tolerant digital systems. The first part, published in November, presented the general principles of fault tolerance and discussed the use of redundancy to increase system reliability and availability. The article also commented on the design of self-testing logic circuits. In this second part, we concentrate more on what has been achieved in practice, and the article describes the JPL-Star computer. This is an experimental computer designed to evaluate many of the strategies for enhancing fault-tolerance, and it is already obsolete. This article concludes, therefore, with a brief survey of other fault-tolerant proposals and implementations

articleTitle: The industrial reality of fibre optics
abstract: Optical-fibre systems show great promise: they have many advantages and many uses can be found for them. The range of components necessary for the systems are available and well proved; engineers should not be afraid of using them

Anyone not directly connected with the manufacture of squirrel-cage induction motors could be forgiven for thinking that this is a product which is virtually dormant in terms of product development. In fact, motor manufacturers face a constant battle to keep their products in line with revisions in international and customer specifications and tighter noise and safety regulations, while making best use of developments in materials to keep costs under control and stay viable

articleTitle: Development of a new video-cassette system
abstract: BCN is the type designation of a broadcast-standard system of video-tape recorders that conforms to modern recording standards. The format has been accepted on a global scale since December 1975 and equipment operating Pal, Secam, and NTSC has been delivered to countries with greatly different climatic conditions

In the computer industry, Gene Amdahl has done the impossible. He has taken on the giant IBM organisation and succeeded. Following a disagreement with IBM management, he set up the Amdahl Corporation in 1970 and has seen its sales of large mainframe IBM compatible computers rocket from virtually zero in 1976 to $320 million in 1978.

British electronics companies are likely to face increasing competition from abroad in the future. If they are to remain successful, they must continue to invent and innovate. To help them to be this, inventions and innovations can be categorised as an aid to selecting areas on which to concentrate inventive talents

`Light rapid transit' is essentially an upgraded tramway; in the popular idiom it is a `supertram'. It is often developedon the basis of a conventional electric tramway, it generally operates on its own segregated right of way, and it incorporates up-to-date equipment based on proven and accepted technology, but without necessarily incurring all the costly system in on the middle ground: betweeen the ordinary street-running transport mode(the bus) and the fully-equipped rapid transit system (the London Underground)

In front of me lie two volumes, Whewell's `Mechanics' published in 1833, and the Cambridge University Calendar for 1834: although so old, they have a considerable bearing on what is wrong with British industry today, since they show how we used to produce educated men until 1848, that revolutionary year in Europe. In that year, a tragedy occurred that has ruined English education, and is now starting to ruin Scottish education too.

articleTitle: Increasing demand for fast p.c.b. throughput
Role of hydrogen in our future fuel supply
abstract: Is water our ultimate fuel source as Jules Verne predicted more than 100 years ago? From water hydrogen can be derived to form the currency of an energy economy that can be generated, transmitted and, most importantly, stored. But what technical and economic conditions have to be fulfilled before a hydrogen economy can be realised?

articleTitle: Hazard reduction in process plant by instrumention philosophy
abstract: Many present-day plant instrumentation, protection and control systems require labour-intensive periodic testing to bolster the user's faith that the systems remain operative. These test arrangements increase costs and can degrade plant safety. Where such apparatus is used in industrial plant, failures may hazard the plant, the environment and life. Such cases arise particularly in the safety aspects of many industrial processes where dangers exist in the form of radiation, toxic substances, high pressure, temperature or energy. Except in special cases, self-testing, fault-tolerance, fail-safe and similar principles have hardly been applied. This article explores these themes which could, with advantage, be applied more widely and in tandem as means of maintaining process plant in safe service and reducing labour-intensive testing procedures by making all faults safely self-proclaiming

The explosive growth of the use of the microcomputer, involving many automated processes now done partly or wholly by hand or by earlier automatic systems, will greatly influence the qualities required of those people working with such systems. Many traditional skills will be supplanted; others will be required. With this scenario, we must radically rethink how we educate children, especially those not destined for higher education and, of equal importance, how we should retrain our existing work force

articleTitle: Industrial expansion and relocation incentives for small firms
abstract: The recognition that small companies make a vital contribution to the national economy and that they should be given every encouragement to expand has had a growing influence in shaping Britain's industrial policy in the past few years

The modern air-defence radar has become a very sophisticated piece of equipment. It has to be if it is to operate successfully in a hostile natural and electronic environment in time of war. But what are the characteristics that need to be incorporated to make the modern Martello Tower effective?

articleTitle: The microprocessor as component and tool
abstract: Some 30 years ago, the invention of the junction transistor and the operation of the first stored-program computer heralded the separate technologies of semiconductor and computer which are now integrated into a common information processing technology as epitomised by the microprocessor. During this period, the electrical engineer has developed an attitude to the computer as a tool which is different from that adopted by the computer designer producing it as a product, made out of an assemblage of components. These components have recently acquired the complexity and nature of computers, microcomputers, and are finding general application in all areas of electrical engineering. The skills and knowledge appropriate for the use of the computer as a tool must now be blended with those appropriate to the design of the computer as a product if the new microprocessor components are to be used effectively by the professional engineer. They provide new opportunities for ingenuity and bring with them new responsibilities to society at large

articleTitle: You can't take it with you-a survey of employed inventor's rights
abstract: An innovative engineer, a highly prized and trusted employee, changes his job or perhaps leaves to set up his own firm. What rights has he to transfer his knowledge from one company to another or to use the knowledge to set up his own company?

Newspapers, which reflect the spirit of their age, should be involved in the upheavals of the contemporary world. After all, we report these upheavals; sometimes we are even accused of creating them. So it is that we become caught up in what I call the `electronic challenge'

The first of British Rail's new Advanced Passenger Trains has recently been seen running on the main line between London and Glasgow. This article describes the new generation of 250 km/h electrically-powered tilting trains

articleTitle: A.C. testing at Project UHV yields useful corona data
abstract: Project UHV (ultra-high voltage) was initiated by the US Electric Research Council in 1967 to study overhead transmission lines with alternating voltages in excess of 1000 kV. Project UHV evolved from Project UHV, the research facility built and funded by General Electric (US) in the period from 1958 to 1964 to provide data for extra-high-voltage transmission in the 400-750 kV range. In the first stage of the project, from 1967 to 1973, a single-phase test line was constructed and energised to define the problems and assess the study priorities. In 1973, Project UHV was transferred to the jurisdiction of the US Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI). A broad spectrum of subjects vital to the design of u.h.v. lines have been studied since. These include air-gap strength, Insulator contamination, switching surge flashover, field effects and corona. This article will discuss some of the results of the corona studies on the prototype transmission line

articleTitle: The swing to electricity: why and how?
abstract: I believe that an overview of the world's energy needs dictates a shift from oil and gas to coal and nuclear fuels as the prime sources for our energy base, and that for both coal and nuclear fuel, electricity is ordinarily the most practical form in which to use them

articleTitle: Bit-slice microprocessors - their use and application in minicomputers
abstract: Although the effort necessary to develop an effective bit-slice-microprocessor microprogrammed design initially seems significant, the benefits far outweigh the investment. After microprogramming techniques are developed, new applications become much easier to accomplish. Although a designer may have to learn new methods, once mastered, a very powerful design tool can be applied to solving complex data processing or control communication systems

articleTitle: Intelsat: facing the problems of success
abstract: After 15 years of successful expansion, the International Telecommunication Satellite organisation (Intelsat) has become a dominant force in international communication, handling two-thirds of the world's transoceanic communication traffic. However, Intelsat's success has brought it a number of problems, both technological and political

articleTitle: Wind-power research and development in the UK
abstract: In the USA, expenditure on windpower research and development has reached $60 million for 1979. Britain is several years behind in terms of expenditure: the USA now has several large machines either working or near completion. But, as Britain is concentrating its efforts on designs and sites, e.g. offshore plant, which the US programme is not covering in great depth, Britain still has something to offer the international research effort

articleTitle: The National Theatre's scenery flying system
abstract: When the National Theatre's point-hoist flying system was being planned, the only other system of its type, that in the BBC Television Centre Studio 1, was to be dismantled: not an auspicious beginning. In the preceding article of this issue, Richard Brett gives an overall view of the electronic systems in the National Theatre; this article looks in detail at the design criteria for the theatre's variable-speed flying system

articleTitle: Approach to the evaluation of microprocessor development systems
abstract: The microprocessor industry is now showing signs of maturity as the methods by which microprocessor-based products are developed are becoming clearly defined. This article is intended to emphasise the need for the correct tools to be used in development. Serious professional work with a microprocessor needs to be undertaken with a healthy understanding of the risks and pitfalls. The author and his colleagues are nearing the completion of a project in which development aids have been studied by in-depth laboratory evaluation. This work shows that a great deal of time and money can be wasted without prudent choice of the correct tools. This article describes the parts of these tools which it is important to evaluate. Microprocessor product development is highly labour intensive and the engineers with the right knowledge and experience are at the moment rare and expensive. It is important therefore to use equipment that is quick and efficient in order to deploy these engineers effectively

Circuit breakers using sulphur-hexafluoride (SF6) gas are finding an increasing share of the world e.h.v. market, mainly because of the advantages they offer the user. These advantages include superior performance, increased contact life, and, with the single-pressure versions of these circuit breakers, simplified construction. However, the introduction of a new technology brings with its advantages a number of problems in design, operation and maintenance, which must be recognised by the designer and user

While examining theses and editing papers, John Carroll, a Reader at the University of Cambridge and one of the Honorary Editors of the IEE Journal on Solid State and Electron Devices, has had many thoughts about the problems of technical writing. In the hope of stimulating thought and discussion about this ever-controversial topic, Dr. Carroll sets out below some of his own views on creating good technical papers

The NEB's latest venture is an attempt to give Britain a world-scale computer-peripherals industry based on a joint venture between British-based Data Recording instruments Co. (DRI) and US computer giant Control Data. Already the largest independent manufacturer of peripherals in Europe, DRI may soon find itself competing head-on with the dominant US peripherals industry.

If coal is to assume its proper place as the major source of hydrocarbons when oil and gas run out, it is important that the world recognises now the urgency for mining industries in every country to receive the support, encouragement and, above all, resources necessary to meet the demands that will inevitably be made on it

Since the turn of this century at least, physics has been dominated by atomic and subatomic phenomena. The search for the fundamental particle has led scientists into a deeper understanding of a world which has brought forth electronics, solid-state physics and the semiconductor devices that exert such a large influence on all aspects of contemporary life. However, mother nature's greatest marvels frequently show scant dependence on the purity of elemental crystals, at least when providing the mechanism for energy conversion or power generation. Here, the complex molecules of organic chemistry hold sway

The advent of the microprocessor has already produced significant changes in the design of instruments, as recent product announcements bear witness. The latest instruments can be seen as the first examples of a whole new generation of `intelligent' instruments that will come onto the market in the next few years

articleTitle: V-M.O.S. improves efficiency through switching performance
abstract: Since the first commercially available 2 A V-metal-oxide-semiconductor (V-m.o.s.) transistor in late 1975, development has been continued by Siliconix and others to extend the current and voltage capabilities of V-m.o.s. and other m.o.s. power structures, which will enable a wider range of application to be achieved in future, especially in the fields of power conversion and motor control. Lower current devices will also be required for general logic interface and signal switching applications, and these areas are not being neglected

articleTitle: A regenerative braking system for d.c. railway traction
abstract: The d.c. motor at present provides most electric railway motive power, and, since the earliest days of electric traction, a great deal of effort has been expended in devising methods of regenerative braking suitable for d.c. systems. The system described here uses a series motor and features an automatic change from weak- to full-field operation. With this method, which was used for the first time in multiple-unit trainsets owned by London Transport and Danish State Railways, continuous blending of rheostatic and regenerative braking can be incorporated at low cost, and every opportunity can be taken to return energy to the supply

articleTitle: HP's instrument philosophy begins at home
abstract: Electronic test and measurement instruments are spanning wider ranges of frequency and amplitude than ever before with greater precision. At the same time, users are expecting instruments to offer improved performance and be easier to use, TONY PRINS talked to WILLIAM E. TERRY, Hewlett-Packard Vice-President and General Manager, Instrument Group, about how his company's instrument range has developed over the years and his philosophy for successful instrument design

articleTitle: In-circuit test techniques cut programming requirements
abstract: Screening printed-circuit cards for assembly and component defects simplifies the entire testing programme.

articleTitle: Flat television display ߝ the shape of things to come
abstract: There is a dream that continues to haunt television engineers: a dream that, one day, they may be able to design and build a truly flat colour television screen. Just why the idea is so attractive it is difficult to say, but there are many research teams in various countries working on the realisation of the dream

articleTitle: Developments in communication at the Open University
abstract: The Open University is undertaking several developments to improve the university's educational process further. The main effort has been directed towards the feedback and remedial components of the system, and the developments include: various computer-based information retrieval and educational systems; a dedicated teleconferencing network; and various uses of a standard t.v. set coupled, for example, to an audio-cassette recorder, a telephone or a lightpen

articleTitle: Sir Joseph Swan and the invention of the electric lamp
abstract: This month, Electronics & Power celebrates the 100th anniversary of the invention of the electric lamp by Sir Joseph Swan. On the 3rd February 1879 in the lecture theatre of the Literary & Philosophical Society at Newcastle, he performed the first practical demonstration of a working lamp. By October of the following year, he was able to light the same auditorium with 20 lamps, the first time any building was lit by incandescent electric lamp.

articleTitle: Whole-body monitoring-the direct determination of radioisotopes within the human body
abstract: In the nuclear industry, it is essential to keep a close watch on the isotopes that the industry's workforce absorbs. Whole-body monitoring determines directly the identity, location and amount of radionuclides in the human body, but it is not the complete answer to the problem. Whole-body monitoring is just part of a complete programme, which should include indirect methods and external dosimetry, to provide a full radiation history of the workforce

articleTitle: An update on the protection of low-voltage a.c. machines
abstract: In any motor drive, satisfactory performance and protection of the operating system depends not only on the protective devices, but also on the capability and reliability of control and switchgear. Thus to optimise a given system, the correct selection of components is of paramount importance

Fields and circuits provide two powerful sets of conceptual tools for the understanding of electrical devices and processes. Both ideas have particular strengths and weaknesses. It is very desirable that students should be taught both methods so that they are able to use either as appropriate

articleTitle: Japanese help to commerce and industry

abstract: Parts 1 and 2 of the Carabian conundrum, concerning the prebid phase of an overseas electronic automation contract, were published in the July and October 1978 issues of E&P. At this point we have decided to pause and present extracts from a selection of the many written replies received. To all those who have made a considerable effort-thank you. The replies printed are not necessarily the best (that would be presumptious on my part), but the points covered reflect other responses

articleTitle: Increasing the advantages of automatic component assembly
abstract: Experience shows that many of the objectives, which industries that have installed automatic assembly processes have sought to attain, can only be achieved when all the problems and immediate needs are fully understood, carefully thought through and effectively solved by those responsible for installing the automated production equipment. Out of the process of solving the problem, it is possible to extract and demonstrate numerous valuable viewpoints, procedures and specific solutions that can help to increase the advantages of automatic assembly machinery to the user

articleTitle: A practical step towards improving attitudes in industry and higher education
abstract: Society still assigns a low value to doing things and getting things done and, although it may slowly be changing its attitude, the process could well do with a push. The absence of constructive suggestions for plausible action is itself a symptom of the difticulty. Perhaps, as this article suggests, the first step is to expose some of the `educators' to situations likely to create a more informed debate towards viable solutions. One day a fortnight in a manufacturing situation is a realistic alternative to research for at least some engineering teachers

articleTitle: The management of microcomputer-based software developments
abstract: The availability of the low-priced microprocessor and other associated large-scale-integration (l.s.i.) devices - `the microprocessor revolution - is not only causing politicians and trade unions to rethink policies and attitudes, and industrialists to plan new strategies, it also means problems for technical and project managers throughout Britain, who now find that the microprocessor is a component part of some new equipment they are currently manufacturing or developing

articleTitle: Pulse-code modulation for broadcast signal distribution
abstract: The reduction in cost and increase in range of digital circuits has meant that, for broadcast signals, as with other aspects of communication engineering, digital processing is an attractive alternative to analogue methods, Sound and vision signals are unlikely to be broadcast in digital form in the near future because, if for no other reason, of the extensive ownership of receivers of analogue signals. However, pulse-code modulation of sound signals for distribution between broadcast centres has been used in different ways for several years. For video signals, development work carried out by broadcasting organisations has yielded promising results

Electroheating by magnetically inducing high-power currents into metal has been an accepted industrial process for over half a century. During the last decade, rapid development in high-current solid-state devices has resulted in the gradual replacement of the motor generator by frequency converters for the generation of medium-frequency power (300 Hz to 10 kHz). Power at these frequencies is normally used for forging, forming and melting, and for deeper case hardening. Lower frequencies (50 to 200 Hz) are obtained straight from supply lines, or from magnetic multipliers; applications include forging and melting at high power levels. Higher frequencies between 100 kHz and 10 MHz are produced by radio-frequency systems, and processes include hardening and joining. This article summarises the main areas of induction heating and the systems used to generate and control these power sources, and includes extracts from a new book on induction heating by the authors, published this summer. Advantages of induction heating include fast and precise heating, clean and compact equipment and, in many instances, cost savings compared with traditional methods

articleTitle: British telecommunication and the information age
abstract: Exactly 110 years after it was given a legal monopoly of telecommunication operation in the UK, the Post Office is now facing what many believe will be its biggest challenge: reconstructing the national telecommunication network to provide the new communication services on which Britain's success in the coming `Information age' will critically depend. How is the Post Office planning to meet the challenge of the new Information technology? And how do its many critics regard its chances of success?

Albert Einstein was born 100 years ago on the 14th March 1879. 26 years later, in 1905, he published three papers, one of which expounded the Special Theory of Relativity. In 1915, he published his General Theory, which predicted the bending of light rays passing near the sun. When, in 1919, the prediction was apparently confirmed experimentally, Einstein achieved great fame. But was all this adulation deserved?

articleTitle: Role of information in human affairs
abstract: During the last two decades, so many electrical engineers have become primarily concerned with the collection, manipulation, communication and use of `information' that the phrase `information engineering' has come into use to denote their activities. About a year ago, Murray Laver delivered a stimulating lecture (on which the article published in may 1979 E&P, p. 329, is based) on the subject of electronics applied to information engineering, in the course of which he made an eloquent plea that the information engineer should not be content to be a neutral artificer concerned only with the mechanics of the processing and communication of information, but that he should also cultivate an awareness of the social purpose of his wares to complement his skills in making them. His plea fell on at least one pair of receptive ears - mine! I propose to try to pick up Murray Laver's challenge and discuss the role of information in human affairs

`As technologies converge, the industries based upon them inevitably collide', as a recent E&P `Focus' article said.* No current technological development is likely to shape our future as much as the convergence of the semiconductor and computer technologies, and this convergence is now inevitably leading to a very real collision between the semiconductor companies and the established computer industry. This collision is shown most clearly by the introduction of minicomputer-like 16-bit `supermicros', which are bringing the semiconductor and minicomputer companies into direct competition. However, this development is just part of the far-reaching confrontation between the two industries

abstract: This year marks the centenary of the independent development by Swan and Edison of the successful incandescent lamp. This device, more than any other, was responsible for the final conquest of the dark ages. However, it was merely one of the last shots in the battle which electric light, in one form or another, had been waging against the forces of darkness since the turn of the 19th century

In the past, the sea has played a uniquely important role in Britain's economy. In the energy-deficient future, the seas seem set to play an equally important role, as providers of renewable alternative energy competing directly with the increasingly troubled nuclear-power programme. Far from being an easy option, however, the exploitation of the sea's vast reserves of natural energy, as embodied in both tidal and wave motion, is now one of the major challenges facing Britain's engineering community

Next month will see the first public showing of System X, the new range of British-made telecommunication switching systems that represents a `make or break' attempt to restore the British telecommunication industry to its former role of being a major force in world telecommunication. System X, however, is not so much a range of specific equipment designs as a whole approach to the problems of telecommunication modernisation that is based on the pooled expertise of the British Post Office and the three main British telecommunication-equipment manufacturers. Impressive as the technical specification of the System X equipment may be, it is the arrangements for uniting the efforts of the four participants, and the new spirit of enterprise that lies behind them, that forms the real strongpoint of the System X venture

articleTitle: Stored energy transmission for road vehicles
abstract: A general-purpose motor vehicle would use less than half the fuel on an average journey if its engine could be properly matched to the task. Proper matching requires an energy store and this should be a flywheel to avoid the need for energy conversion and the consequent losses. The difficulties in using a small geared-up flywheel for such a purpose lie-mainly in its control, but these can now be solved with the help of large-scale-integration of digital circuitry. To illustrate these principles, a stored-energy transmission system is described which offers several advantages in addition to fuel saving

articleTitle: Review of potential hydroelectric development in the Scottish Highlands
abstract: Current discussion surrounding the energy problem gives constant reference to the contribution of renewable power sources. Although limited in scope, this article attempts to identify the remaining exploitable hydroelectric potential within the Scottish Highlands, and to suggest how such development with the use of known technology could realise substantial benefits to this sparsely inhabited region

articleTitle: The electric lamp business. Part 1: Edison and the gas companies
abstract: The electrical industry was born into an era of cheap coal and readily available steam power, so that for many years the only service that electricity could hope to offer in competition with its established rivals was the provision of cheap and convenient lighting. The whole industry was thus dependent on the success of electric lighting, and on the profits of the electric-lamp business in particular. The story of the electric-lamp business, from the pioneering days of Swan and Edison to the international price-fixing rings of the 1930s, is thus the story of the birth and adolescence of the whole electrical industry

articleTitle: Windmills on the mind: a study in dynamics and control
The electric lamp business. Part 2: War of the lamps
abstract: Edison's work on electric lighting, which shaped the future of the whole electrical industry, was guided by one clear aim: `to effect [an] exact imitation of all done by gas, to replace lighting by gas by lighting by electricity'. The early development of the electrical industry was based on the simple strategy of using the superiority of the electric lamp to drive the gas companies out of the highly profitable lighting market. For over a decade this strategy worked, but then the gas companies hit back with a new form of gas lighting that neatly turned the tables on the electric lamp. This new threat to electrical development delayed the final triumph of the electrical industry for nearly 20 years

abstract: In one respect, the Second Work War did a disservice to control engineering, since it gave rise to textbooks that ignored the historical development of control science in the preceding centuries. Yet the structure of controllers designed by modem theories often turns out to resemble that found by investigators in the 19th century, or even earlier. Consequently, control engineers have begun taking a belated interest in the history of their subject. The present book is the first in English to attempt a broad account of the development of control engineering during the period 1800-1930.
